title: The user schema
idea: A Mongoose schema lists a document's fields, types and rules. The model built from it reads and writes one MongoDB collection.

analogy.text: A registration form at a front desk. The clerk tidies each answer and refuses blank required boxes; the filing cabinet rejects a second card with the same name.
analogy.breaks: MongoDB never sees the form; Mongoose enforces it inside your app.

points: Each field takes a `type` and rules such as `required`, `default`, `trim` and `lowercase`.
`trim` and `lowercase` run when a value is set; `required` is checked on save.
`unique: true` asks MongoDB for a unique index; MongoDB, not Mongoose, rejects duplicates.
Unknown fields are dropped; `timestamps: true` adds `createdAt` and `updatedAt`.

steps.caption: A sign-up arrives with a padded, upper-case username and a `role` field that the schema does not list.
Setters run as the document is built. `trim` and `lowercase` clean the username; the unknown `role` is dropped.
out: role: dropped, not in the schema

steps.caption: `save()` runs the validators. Every `required` field is present, so the document moves on.
out: role: dropped, not in the schema

steps.caption: Mongoose adds `createdAt` and `updatedAt`. MongoDB inserts the document and records `ada` in the unique index.
out: role: dropped, not in the schema

steps.caption: The user is stored. `isEmailVerified` is `false` because of its `default`.
out: role: dropped, not in the schema

steps.caption: A second user signs up as `ADA`. Setters make it `ada` and validation passes, so MongoDB checks its unique index.
The index already holds `ada`. MongoDB rejects the insert with code 11000, which is not a `ValidationError`.
A sign-up with no `username` fails `required`. Mongoose throws a `ValidationError` and never contacts MongoDB.

code.title: src/models/user.models.js
code.caption: The whole model. A field is optional unless it says `required`.

walk.text: `username` is required and unique. `lowercase` and `trim` clean it when it is set.
`email` has the same rules, so `Ada@Mail.com` and `ada@mail.com` collide.
`required` can take `[true, message]` to set the error text. The next lesson hashes the password.
Token and expiry fields stay empty until the token flows fill them in.
`timestamps: true` adds `createdAt` and `updatedAt` and keeps them current.
`mongoose.model` returns the model. Its documents live in the `users` collection.

code.title: The rules in action
code.caption: A smaller schema with the same rules, run on real MongoDB. The password is plain text here; the next lesson hashes it.

walk.text: `username` carries the same four rules as in the model.
`required` can carry the error message as `[true, message]`.
Connect, then `init()` waits until the unique index exists.
The messy input comes back clean: `role` is dropped, and the default and timestamps appear.
An empty user fails `required`: a `ValidationError` with your message, and nothing reaches MongoDB.
`ADA` becomes `ada`, which exists already. MongoDB rejects it with code 11000.

pitfalls: `unique` builds an index, not a validator: catch error code `11000` on duplicates.
Never pass `req.body` straight to `User.create`: a client could send `isEmailVerified: true`.
Do not return a whole user document: it carries `password` and the token fields.

quiz.why: Setters run when the document is built: `trim` and `lowercase` give `ada`. `role` is not in the schema, so Mongoose drops it.

takeaway: A schema cleans and checks data; only the index stops duplicates.

starters: Why does `lowercase` matter for a `unique` username?
Why is the collection called `users` and not `User`?
Can I add a field to the schema after users already exist?
